thing: The Grasshopper (Suits' book) qua riddle-solving game
quote: there is another useful sense in which The Grasshopper is at once a game and an artwork — a lovely work of art, at that.
why: VERIFIED verbatim, contiguous. Predication in Ridge's own voice in his concluding paragraph, not a report: he introduces it as 'I cannot resist concluding by illustrating the compatibility of being a game and being an artwork with none other than Suits' The Grasshopper' and then says in his own voice 'it is a riddle-solving game, in which the lusory goals are to solve certain riddles'. He leans on Kolers but endorses ('has, to my mind, plausibly argued'); the residual hedge 'if Kolers is right' attaches to the mereological claim about which rules are parts, not to the game-status claim. The 'artwork' half of the quote is a separate question and is not what is tagged.

quote: If, however, we understand the prescription to make and appreciate beautiful moves as not being part of chess, but rather what makes chess an artwork (or, perhaps, a medium for artworks) as well as a game, we can avoid such awkward consequences.
why: VERIFIED verbatim, contiguous. Ridge's own preferred position ('If, however, we understand...we can avoid such awkward consequences'), and 'as well as a game' predicates gamehood of chess — a thing can only be an artwork 'as well as a game' if it is a game. Weaker in form than a bare predication because the sentence's main business is the artwork side, but the game predication is Ridge's, not Rough's, and is corroborated throughout ('In chess, the rules of the game include...', 'In chess, the goal is to give checkmate').

thing: playing chess while caring only about winning (no aesthetic concern)

quote: That, though, is absurd; the chess player who only cares about winning is still playing chess.
why: VERIFIED verbatim, contiguous. Polarity checked: this is Ridge asserting, against a consequence he attributes to Rough's mereology ('would wrongly predict...that someone who did not care about beauty in chess was thereby not really playing chess'). The view being attacked is the negative; Ridge's own position is the positive, marked by 'That, though, is absurd'. An activity case in the family of 'obeying traffic rules for their own sake': the assertion is that the activity is still an instance of playing that game. Discriminating against definitions that load the lusory attitude with aesthetic requirements.

quote: It may be that a child is punished by not being allowed to play games, but this has no bearing on the ontological status of Monopoly, even if the parental restriction overrides the game’s prescription that one play it with the lusory attitude.
why: Rough's own voice, not a reported view, and not a list-of-examples mention: he takes a position on Monopoly's ontological status, holding that an external (parental) restriction overriding its lusory-attitude prescription leaves that status untouched. Gamehood is carried inside the sentence by "the game’s prescription that one play it with the lusory attitude" — "the game" is Monopoly — so the paper asserts Monopoly is, and remains, a game. It functions as the contrast case to the Fountain/urinal discussion immediately preceding: restrictions internal/constitutive to the object can change what it is, external ones cannot. Caveat for the record: the gamehood is designated in passing ("the game’s prescription") while the asserted content is about ontological status, so this is an assertion resting on a presupposed designation rather than a bare "Monopoly is a game" sentence.

quote: if we  wish to give thoughtful consideration to the claims of those who play games (including  chess players are who also artists and art critics — Marcel Duchamp and William  Wimsatt among them)
why: VERIFIED verbatim, contiguous, below the marker. Myers's own voice (his closing argument, not a paraphrase of Rough): chess players are given as members of "those who play games", which classifies chess as a game rather than merely mentioning it. Corroborated by a second own-voice line I also verified as present in the text, "chess players frequently advocate for the play of their game as art" ("their game" = chess). Deliberately NOT quoted: "a bona fide (non-video-game) game such as chess", because that phrase sits inside Myers's paraphrase of Rough's two interlocking claims and would be an attributed view. The rest of the sentence concerns whether chess players are ARTISTS — an artwork claim, not tagged here. The paper's own typo "chess players are who also artists" is preserved.

thing: This War of Mine (11 bit studios, 2014)
quote: This more generic  claim could then avoid being immediately burdened with distinguishing between what  on occasion might be called a video game (e. g. This War of Mine) from what upon occasion might not be called a video game (e. g., This War of Mine).
why: VERIFIED verbatim, contiguous, below the marker. Myers's own voice: he names This War of Mine as the example on BOTH sides of the classification and explicitly proposes a framing that avoids having to settle it, consistent with his stated refusal to "account for all possible uses of the term 'game' or the term 'video game'" (that surrounding line is context only — a hyphenated line-break runs through it, so it cannot serve as a quote). Hence U, not P or N. Two caveats recorded honestly: (a) the undecidedness is worded over "video game", and in this exchange video-game-hood is not simply game-hood (Rough, as Myers reports him, contrasts video games with "a bona fide (non-video-game) game such as chess") — the tag rests on the paper treating both terms in parallel as ones it declines to adjudicate; (b) the back matter has a reference heading "Games" listing "11 bit studios (2014). This War of Mine. Windows.", a bibliographic pull toward P, but a section heading is not an assertion and no own-voice sentence anywhere states that This War of Mine is a game.

Not a bare mention: Donkey Kong is the paradigm case the whole article analyses, and the analysis treats it as having exactly the two parts the authors take a game to have — a rule system and a fictional world ("In Donkey Kong, we can call upon the rules of the game and that the game would be too difficult otherwise"). Verbatim check passes on the normalised text.

quote: he is surely correct that tabletop fantasy role-playing is a game and not a simulation
why: Garthoff's clearest gamehood predication, endorsed in his own voice ("he is surely correct"). Verified verbatim. Two caveats recorded rather than hidden: (a) the endorsement is scoped by the preceding "Understood this way", i.e. granted on the construal of realism as simulated experience — but the commitment is independently confirmed throughout the paper, which calls tabletop role-playing games games without qualification; (b) the contrast term is 'simulation', not 'game', so only the positive half is a GAME case, and fn. 22 ("Tabletop role-playing games are simulations in this sense") qualifies the simulation half, not the gamehood half. Juul's contrary borderline-case view at fn. 48 is reported and rejected, not endorsed.

quote: By contrast the first edition of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons is, to this day,  among the most complex games in the genre.
why: Verified verbatim (double space after the line break preserved). "is ... among the most complex games in the genre" predicates gamehood directly, in Garthoff's own voice, and the sentence's own claim is about AD&D's standing as a game. Corroborated elsewhere ("Even if first edition Advanced Dungeons & Dragons is the superior game"; "that most majestically unplayable game"), so it is not the reading of one stray phrase. Gygax's view that it is a wholly separate game is reported, but that is not what is tagged.

quote: The first role-playing game, Dungeons & Dragons, was co-created by Dave Arneson  and Gary Gygax and published in 1974.
why: Verified verbatim. Explicit appositive predication: D&D is the first role-playing game. Asserted by Garthoff as a historical claim of the essay, not reported from a source (the citation at fn. 4 is to the game itself and to Peterson's history, not to a rival view).

quote: Live-action role-playing  grew out of tabletop role-playing, becoming its own genre of game with much greater  emphasis on realism of simulated experience.
why: Verified verbatim. "becoming its own genre of game" asserts gamehood of LARP specifically. Polarity checked: Garthoff's later insistence that LARP is "a very different activity from tabletop role-playing", and that realism constrains it differently, is a difference-of-activity claim and not a denial of gamehood, so P is right rather than N or U.

quote: As the success of GURPS and other highly playable games suggests

"GURPS and other highly playable games" entails GURPS is one of the games, asserted in Garthoff's own voice as a premise of his argument that AD&D 1e overreaches toward realism. Noted for the record: elsewhere he calls GURPS a role-playing 'system' rather than a game, but that is a looser usage and does not contradict this predication.

quote: A far less realistic  game – such as the gothic-themed Vampire: The Masquerade, which briefly surpassed  Advanced Dungeons & Dragons in sales during the nadir of the latter game’s popularity  in the 1990s – might be superior by this standard.

The evaluative half (that it might be superior by the diversion/amusement standard) is a separate claim and is not what is tagged. thing_he left null rather than inventing a Hebrew title.

The marginality the original tagger flagged does not disqualify it: the sentence explicitly predicates, in Garthoff's own voice, that the 2000 overhaul "constituted a new game" and that this new game is what was labeled the third edition — gamehood is asserted, not merely presupposed by an identity claim. Independent of the other six cases.

(verified) and, in footnote 4, "chess, the game that will never be fully solved" (verified).

quote: Games exist neither as player, nor chess board, nor chess piece, or chess rule, instead, they put these relata into a distinctive, meaningful relationship and assume an existence in their own right.
why: Verified verbatim and contiguous. The paper's own thesis, stated in the first person elsewhere ("I am going to argue that games, as processes of play, appear in the figure of this 'in-between'"): game-hood is explicitly denied of four named concrete relata — the board, the piece, the rule, the player. Thing widened from the original tagger's "board (and pieces)" because the same sentence names the chess rule.

quote: As each game constructs its own system of causality, these modes of attention usually lack clear applications in non-game environments. A strategic chess mind will not automatically succeed in strategic business planning since chess and business operate according to wildly different laws.

Business is the instance the author supplies for the "non-game environments" named in the immediately preceding sentence, and it is contrasted with chess as operating under different laws. FLAG: the words "business is not a game" never appear — the denial is carried by apposition of the example to "non-game environments", one inferential step.
